### Node Version

22.17.1

### Package Manager

yarn

### Package Manager Version

 1.22.22

### Strapi Version

5.52.3

### Operating System

Windows 11

### Database

Strapi Cloud

### Javascript or Typescript

Javascript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

Selecting a `private: true` attribute inside a nested `populate` via the Document Service throws `ValidationError: Invalid key <attr>` (400), while selecting the same attribute with top-level `fields` works.

This is a re-report of #23361, which was closed by the stale bot without a fix. The root cause is a key mismatch between `@strapi/core` and `@strapi/utils`:

`@strapi/core/dist/services/document-service/repository.js` passes the nested-populate validations under the key `field` (singular):

```js
const populateValidations = {
  sort: sortValidations,
  field: fieldValidations,        // ['scalarAttributes']
  filters: filtersValidations,
  populate: ['nonAttributesOperators'],
};
```

But `validatePopulate` in `@strapi/utils/dist/validate/validators.js` reads `includes.fields` (plural) for nested `fields`:

```js
if (key === 'fields') {
  set(key, await validateFields({ schema, getModel }, value, includes?.fields || FIELDS_TRAVERSALS));
}
```

`includes.fields` is always undefined, so it falls back to `FIELDS_TRAVERSALS` (`scalarAttributes`, `privateFields`, `passwordFields`). As a result, internal Document Service queries get the Content API's private-field restriction, but only for nested populate fields.

Per the docs, `private` only removes an attribute from server responses. It should not prevent backend code from reading the attribute through the Document Service.

Still present in 5.53.0, 5.54.0 and 5.55.0.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Content type `organization` with an attribute marked private:
   ```json
   "status": { "type": "enumeration", "enum": ["active", "suspended"], "private": true }
   ```
2. Content type `organization-member` with a relation `organization` → `api::organization.organization`.
3. In backend code (service/controller/policy):
   ```js
   await strapi.documents('api::organization-member.organization-member').findFirst({
     populate: { organization: { fields: ['documentId', 'status'] } },
   });
   ```
   → throws `ValidationError: Invalid key status` (`details: { key: 'status', path: 'status' }`).
4. For comparison, this works:
   ```js
   await strapi.documents('api::organization.organization').findFirst({
     fields: ['documentId', 'status'],
   });
   ```

### Expected Behavior

Nested populate `fields` should be validated with the repository's field validations (`scalarAttributes` only), the same as top-level `fields`. Private attributes should be selectable by internal Document Service calls. Content API validation is unaffected, since it goes through `defaultValidatePopulate`.

### Logs

```shell
ValidationError: Invalid key status
    at Object.throwInvalidKey (@strapi/utils/dist/validate/utils.js:10:11)
    at visitor (@strapi/utils/dist/validate/visitors/throw-private.js:12:15)
    at traverse (@strapi/utils/dist/traverse/factory.js:68:19)
    at @strapi/utils/dist/traverse/query-fields.js:12:44
    at async @strapi/utils/dist/validate/validators.js:453:22
```

### Code Snippets

Suggested one-line fix in `@strapi/utils` `validatePopulate` (we currently ship it as a patch-package patch):

```diff
-            }, value, includes?.fields || FIELDS_TRAVERSALS));
+            }, value, includes?.fields || includes?.field || FIELDS_TRAVERSALS));
```

Alternatively, rename the key in `@strapi/core`'s `populateValidations` from `field` to `fields`.

### Media

_No response_

### Additional information

Workaround: use `strapi.db.query()` (Query Engine) instead of the Document Service for these lookups, or apply the patch above.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
items.title: Document Service rejects private attributes in nested populate `fields` ("Invalid key") — validator reads `includes.fields` but repository passes `field`

### Node Version

24.8.0

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

11.6.0

### Strapi Version

5.48.0

### Operating System

Linux (Other)

### Database

SQLite

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

A Content API route that requires authentication (`config: { auth: {} }`) returns **500 Internal Server Error** when called with **no `Authorization` header**, instead of **401 Unauthorized** (or 403). This happens whenever **any public permission** exists in the users-permissions plugin — which is the default out-of-the-box state (the plugin ships public permissions for its own `/api/auth/*` routes).

An invalid JWT correctly returns 401, and a valid JWT returns 200. The only broken case is "no token at all", which makes this easy to miss. Also still present in the latest release (5.54.0) and on Strapi Cloud.

The 500 body is `{"data":null,"error":{"status":500,"name":"InternalServerError","message":"Internal Server Error"}}`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a fresh Strapi 5 app with the **users-permissions** plugin (default setup — public permissions for the plugin's own auth routes exist out of the box).
2. Add a content API with a protected route:

```ts
// src/api/foo/routes/foo.ts
export default {
  routes: [
    {
      method: "GET",
      path: "/foo",
      handler: "foo.find",
      config: { auth: {} },
    },
  ],
};
```

3. Request it:

```bash
# no Authorization header → 500 (expected 401)
curl -s -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/foo

# invalid JWT → 401 (correct)
curl -s -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/foo -H 'Authorization: Bearer invalid'

# valid JWT → 200 (correct)
curl -s -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/foo -H 'Authorization: Bearer <jwt>'
```

4. Observe the 500 and the error in the server log (see Logs).

### Expected Behavior

A request to a protected route with **no credentials** should return **401 Unauthorized** (or 403), matching the invalid-JWT case. It should never surface as a 500.

### Logs

```shell
error: Forbidden access
ForbiddenError: Forbidden access
    at Object.verify (node_modules/@strapi/plugin-users-permissions/dist/server/strategies/users-permissions.js)
    at Object.verify (node_modules/@strapi/core/dist/services/auth/index.js)
    at node_modules/@strapi/core/dist/services/server/compose-endpoint.js
http: GET /api/foo (14 ms) 500
```

### Code Snippets

`@strapi/core` — `dist/services/server/compose-endpoint.js`, `createAuthorizeMiddleware`:

```js
} catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof strapiUtils.errors.UnauthorizedError) {
        return ctx.unauthorized();
    }
    if (error instanceof strapiUtils.errors.ForbiddenError) {
        ...
        return ctx.forbidden();
    }
    throw error;
}
```

Two compounding bugs:

1. **`instanceof` checks across separate `@strapi/utils` copies never match.** `@strapi/plugin-users-permissions@5.48.0` declares its own `@strapi/utils` dependency, so npm **nests a second copy** (5.48.0) while the top-level copy consumed by `@strapi/core` is 5.46.0. The plugin's `verify` strategy instantiates `ForbiddenError`/`UnauthorizedError` from *its* copy, so the `instanceof` checks in `@strapi/core` are **always false**. The error falls through to `throw error` → global error handler → 500. (Confirmed: `new nestedCopy.UnauthorizedError() instanceof topCopy.UnauthorizedError === false`.)

2. **`ctx.unauthorized()` / `ctx.forbidden()` throw.** Even when the `instanceof` check does match (e.g. errors thrown from `@strapi/core` itself), Koa's `ctx.unauthorized()`/`ctx.forbidden()` *throw* a Koa HTTP error rather than ending the request. Inside the composed route middleware this throw propagates to the global error handler and surfaces as a 500.

3. **(Design question) 403 vs 401 for unauthenticated callers.** With public permissions present, the users-permissions `authenticate` strategy returns `{ authenticated: true, credentials: null, ability }` for token-less requests. Because `auth: {}` routes get an auto-generated scope (`api::<api>.<controller>.<action>`), `verify` never reaches its `!user → UnauthorizedError` branch; instead the public ability check fails with `ForbiddenError` (403). HTTP semantics say a request providing **no credentials** should be 401, reserving 403 for authenticated-but-not-allowed callers.

**Suggested fix:**

- In `createAuthorizeMiddleware`, don't rely on `instanceof` across package boundaries (match on `error.name`, or ensure a single hoisted `@strapi/utils`), and/or replace `return ctx.unauthorized()` / `return ctx.forbidden()` with a direct response:

```js
ctx.status = 401;
ctx.body = { data: null, error: { status: 401, name: error.name, message: error.message, details: error.details || {} } };
return;
```

- In the users-permissions strategy `verify`, throw `UnauthorizedError` when `!user` (no real credentials) and the scope check fails, keeping `ForbiddenError` for genuinely authenticated users.

### Media

_No response_

### Additional information

We are currently working around this with `patch-package` patches to `@strapi/core` + `@strapi/plugin-users-permissions` (match errors by name + set 401/403 directly + 401 for credential-less callers). Happy to share the patches or provide a minimal LaunchPad reproduction if that would speed things up.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
items.title: [Bug] Content API returns 500 instead of 401/403 when route auth fails with public permissions present (users-permissions)

### Node Version

v22.20.0

### Package Manager

yarn

### Package Manager Version

4.12.0

### Strapi Version

`develop` after #26909 (`38ed6a5e2b`). Also seen on `@strapi/database@0.0.0-experimental.c71ae4bb75d293c00fa800dc32eb58ee5c6f95b3` (5.55.0 candidate).

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

SQLite

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

`strapi.db.query(uid).updateMany()` ignores `_q` and `filters`. It only applies `where` and `data`. `deleteMany` and `count` already pick `_q`, `where`, and `filters`.

The path is `packages/core/database/src/entity-manager/index.ts` `updateMany`. It used `{ where, data }` and called `.where(where).update(data)`. `deleteMany` uses `.init(pick(['_q', 'where', 'filters'], params))`.

This is not a regression of #26909. Query-builder `init({ _q, where }).update()` already works. Entity-manager `updateMany` never forwarded those keys.

Found while checking #26909 against the QA comment on that PR. Related: #11998, #23129, #25420, #26909.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a collection with several rows. Example names: `Hugo LLORIS`, `Lucas HERNANDEZ`, `Samuel UMTITI`.
2. Call `strapi.db.query(uid).updateMany({ _q: 'Hugo', data: { name: 'Q UPDATED' } })`.
3. Read the returned `count` and the remaining names.

### Expected Behavior

Only the row that matches `_q: 'Hugo'` is updated. `count` is `1`. Remaining names: `Lucas HERNANDEZ`, `Q UPDATED`, `Samuel UMTITI`.

The same narrowing must apply for `filters` and for `_q` or `filters` combined with a relation `where`.

### Logs

```
updateMany({ _q: 'Hugo', data: { name: 'Q UPDATED' } })
count=3
```

Expected `count=1`. Every row was updated.

### Code Snippets

```js
await strapi.db.query('api::test.test').updateMany({
  _q: 'Hugo',
  data: { name: 'Q UPDATED' },
});
```

Coverage added in `tests/api/core/database/db.test.api.js`:

- `updateMany: _q updates matching rows only`
- `updateMany: _q + relation where updates matching rows only`
- `updateMany: filters + relation where updates matching rows only`

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

---

items.body:
### Node Version

v24.7.0

### Package Manager

Yarn

### Package Manager Version

4.17.0

### Strapi Version

5.53.0

### Operating System

Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

In the Media Library edit dialog, cropping an existing (remote) asset right after **Replace media** — without saving first — shows a broken image and the cropper never starts. Saving the replacement first, reopening the asset and then cropping works fine.

The cause is that the crop-time cache-busting parameter is appended to the local `blob:` object URL created for the pending replacement file, which produces a blob URL the browser cannot resolve.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Upload an image to the Media Library.
2. Open the asset, click **Replace media** and pick a new image. The preview updates to the new file.
3. Without saving, click the **Crop** button.
4. The preview turns into a broken image, no crop box appears, and the browser reports a failed request for a URL like `blob:http://localhost:1337/6f0a…?updatedAt=2026-09-21T09%3A12%3A33.000Z`.

Cropping the same asset after saving the replacement works as expected.

### Expected Behavior

Cropping a just-replaced (not yet saved) image should work the same as cropping a saved one.

### Code Snippets

`packages/core/upload/admin/src/components/EditAssetDialog/PreviewBox/PreviewBox.tsx`

When a replacement file is selected, the preview URL becomes a local object URL:

```ts
React.useEffect(() => {
  if (replacementFile) {
    const fileLocalUrl = URL.createObjectURL(replacementFile);
    if (asset.isLocal) {
      asset.url = fileLocalUrl;
    }
    setAssetUrl(fileLocalUrl);
    setThumbnailUrl(fileLocalUrl);
  }
}, [replacementFile, asset]);
```

While cropping, the image is loaded from `cropUrl` rather than `assetUrl`:

```ts
const cropUrl = React.useMemo(() => {
  if (!asset.isLocal && !asset.isUrlSigned && assetUrl) {
    return appendSearchParamsToUrl({ url: assetUrl, params: { updatedAt: asset.updatedAt } });
  }
  return assetUrl;
}, [assetUrl, asset.isLocal, asset.isUrlSigned, asset.updatedAt]);
```

The guard only checks `asset.isLocal`, which is `false` for an existing Media Library asset, so the branch also runs when `assetUrl` is currently the `blob:` URL of the pending replacement. A blob URL is resolved by exact string match against the browser's blob store, so appending a query string produces a URL that does not resolve:

```
blob:http://localhost:1337/6f0a-…  ->  blob:http://localhost:1337/6f0a-…?updatedAt=2026-09-21T09%3A12%3A33.000Z
```

The image fails to load, `onLoad` never fires, `isCropImageReady` stays `false`, and `crop()` is therefore never called.

Suggested fix — exclude object URLs from the cache-busting branch, since they are local and never cross-origin, so they need no cache busting:

```diff
-    if (!asset.isLocal && !asset.isUrlSigned && assetUrl) {
+    if (!asset.isLocal && !asset.isUrlSigned && assetUrl && !assetUrl.startsWith('blob:')) {
```

### Additional information

The code is unchanged on `main` at the time of writing.

We are running this one-line change as a local patch on 5.53.0; cropping a just-replaced image works again, and cropping a saved remote asset still behaves as before. Happy to open a PR if that helps.

Reported by an editor on Chrome 153 / Windows 11 against a Strapi instance running on Linux.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [X] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [X] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
items.title: Media Library: cropping right after "Replace media" breaks because the cache-busting param is appended to the blob: URL

items.body:
### Node Version

22.23.2

### Package Manager

pnpm

### Package Manager Version

11.26.0

### Strapi Version

5.54.0

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Bug Description

Published `@strapi/*` packages ship `.d.ts` files that import modules their own `package.json` does not declare. In a consumer whose `node_modules` is not hoisted, those imports do not resolve, and the types they carry silently become `any`.

The visible symptom in consumer code is implicit-any errors that point at the consumer's own files, with nothing obviously wrong at the Strapi boundary:

```
Type '(props: ErrorProps) => any' is not assignable to type 'never'.
Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'never'.
```

`Page.Error` is typed as returning `any`, and `Core.MiddlewareHandler`'s context is `unknown` instead of a Koa context. Every prop type derived from React collapses the same way.

The cause is that TypeScript resolves a package's imports relative to where that package physically lives, and ignores `NODE_PATH`. When a package is linked from a store outside the consuming repo, the upward directory walk from its `.d.ts` never reaches the consumer's `node_modules`, so `react` resolves to the untyped `react/index.js` rather than to `@types/react`.

This has not surfaced before because two things hide it. A hoisted `node_modules` resolves the missing declarations by accident, and `skipLibCheck: true` — the default in Strapi's own generated `tsconfig.json` — suppresses the errors inside the `.d.ts` files themselves. It is visible to any consumer on pnpm's global virtual store (`enableGlobalVirtualStore`) or Yarn PnP.

One downstream repo hit 28 hard TypeScript errors across their Strapi app and all four of their plugins from this, and now carries 11 `packageExtensions` entries as a workaround.

### Steps to Reproduce

Four files, then one command. This is self-contained and needs no Strapi app.

1. `package.json`

   ```json
   {
     "name": "strapi-types-repro",
     "private": true,
     "version": "1.0.0",
     "dependencies": {
       "@strapi/admin": "5.54.0",
       "@strapi/types": "5.54.0",
       "@strapi/logger": "5.54.0",
       "react": "^18.3.1",
       "react-dom": "^18.3.1",
       "react-router-dom": "^6.30.3",
       "styled-components": "^6.1.13",
       "@types/react": "^18.3.2",
       "@types/react-dom": "^18.3.0",
       "@types/koa": "^2.15.2",
       "@types/lodash": "^4.14.197",
       "typescript": "5.9.3"
     }
   }
   ```

   Note that `@types/react`, `@types/koa` and `@types/lodash` **are** installed at the consumer root. The problem is that the `@strapi/*` packages cannot see them.

2. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` — these keys must go here. pnpm 11 ignores them in `.npmrc`.

   ```yaml
   enableGlobalVirtualStore: true
   nodeLinker: isolated
   hoist: false
   ```

3. `tsconfig.json` — `moduleResolution: Bundler` matches the profile Strapi's own packages are built with.

   ```json
   {
     "compilerOptions": {
       "target": "ESNext",
       "module": "ESNext",
       "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
       "lib": ["DOM", "DOM.Iterable", "ESNext"],
       "jsx": "react-jsx",
       "strict": true,
       "esModuleInterop": true,
       "skipLibCheck": false,
       "noEmit": true,
       "types": []
     },
     "include": ["src"]
   }
   ```

4. `src/probe.tsx` — assigning to `never` makes `tsc` print the type it actually inferred.

   ```tsx
   import type { Core } from '@strapi/types';
   import { Page } from '@strapi/admin/strapi-admin';

   export const showPageError: never = null as unknown as typeof Page.Error;
   export const showCtx: never = null as unknown as Parameters<Core.MiddlewareHandler>[0];
   ```

Then:

```console
$ pnpm install
$ readlink node_modules/@strapi/admin
../../../../../../../../../Users/me/Library/pnpm/store/v11/links/@strapi/admin/5.54.0/…/node_modules/@strapi/admin

$ npx tsc -p .
```

**Observed — 665 errors**, of which 139 originate inside the `@strapi/*` packages:

```
src/probe.tsx: Type '(props: ErrorProps) => any' is not assignable to type 'never'.
src/probe.tsx: Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'never'.

react/index.js' implicitly has an 'any' type.          ×495
react/jsx-runtime.js' implicitly has an 'any' type.    ×112
lodash/lodash.js' implicitly has an 'any' type.        ×12
koa/dist/koa.mjs' implicitly has an 'any' type.        ×8

@strapi/logger :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'logform' or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/types  :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'lodash'  or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/types  :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'undici'  or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/admin  :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'redux'   or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/admin  :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'redux-thunk' or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/admin  :: TS2307: Cannot find module '@remix-run/router' or its corresponding type declarations.
@strapi/admin  :: TS2307: Cannot find module 'formidable' or its corresponding type declarations.
```

`tsc --traceResolution` shows `koa` landing on `koa/dist/koa.mjs` rather than on `@types/koa/index.d.ts`.

Setting `hoist: true`, or switching to npm/yarn defaults, makes all of it disappear — which is the point: the declarations are only correct by accident of layout.

### Expected Behavior

`Page.Error` resolves to `(props: ErrorProps) => Element`, `Core.MiddlewareHandler`'s parameter resolves to a Koa context, and `tsc` reports no errors originating inside the `@strapi/*` packages — the same result a hoisted install already gives today.

In other words, type checking a consumer should not depend on the consumer's `node_modules` layout, and `skipLibCheck: false` should be safe to turn on.

### Additional information

I audited the built `dist/**/*.d.ts` of the core packages at 5.54.0 against their declared dependencies, rather than working from the errors alone. Three groups came out. `dev-only` means the entry is a `devDependency` — declared for the monorepo's own build, but never shipped to consumers.

**1. `@types/*` referenced by the declarations but not declared**

| Package | Missing |
| --- | --- |
| `@strapi/admin` | `@types/react`, `@types/koa`, `@types/qs`, `@types/formidable`; dev-only: `@types/lodash`, `@types/json-logic-js`, `@types/passport-local` |
| `@strapi/core` | `@types/qs`, `@types/jsonwebtoken`; dev-only: `@types/koa`, `@types/lodash`, `@types/http-errors`, `@types/koa__router`, `@types/koa-compress`, `@types/json-logic-js` |
| `@strapi/types` | dev-only: `@types/koa`, `@types/koa__router`, `@types/lodash`, `@types/json-logic-js` |
| `@strapi/utils` | `@types/lodash`; dev-only: `@types/http-errors` |
| `@strapi/permissions` | `@types/lodash` |
| `@strapi/database` | `@types/lodash` |
| `@strapi/email` | `@types/react`; dev-only: `@types/koa` |
| `@strapi/upload` | `@types/react`, `@types/koa`, `@types/formidable` |
| `@strapi/content-manager` | `@types/react`, `@types/koa`, `@types/markdown-it`, `@types/codemirror5`; dev-only: `@types/lodash`, `@types/prismjs` |
| `@strapi/content-type-builder` | `@types/react`, `@types/koa`, `@types/json-logic-js` |
| `@strapi/strapi` | `@types/cli-progress`; dev-only: `@types/inquirer` |

**2. Real modules that leak into inferred return types.** These come from `tsc`'s inference rather than from any hand-written import, which is why they are easy to miss in review.

| Package | Missing | Currently resolves through |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@strapi/admin` | `redux`, `redux-thunk` | `react-redux` + `@reduxjs/toolkit` |
| `@strapi/admin` | `@remix-run/router` | `react-router-dom@6` |
| `@strapi/admin` | `reselect`, `msw` | hoisting |
| `@strapi/types` | `undici` | declared by `@strapi/core`, used by `@strapi/types` |
| `@strapi/logger` | `logform` | `winston` |
| `@strapi/upload` | `reselect`, `redux`, `axios`, `@dnd-kit/utilities` | hoisting |
| `@strapi/content-manager` | `redux` | hoisting |
| `@strapi/content-type-builder` | `redux`, `axios`, `json-logic-js` | hoisting |

**3. Cross-references between `@strapi/*` packages.** `@strapi/email`, `@strapi/upload` and `@strapi/content-type-builder` reference `@strapi/types` in their published declarations and reach it only through the `@strapi/admin` peer. `@strapi/admin` and `@strapi/content-manager` reference `@strapi/database` the same way.

**A possible shape for the fix**, if it is useful — happy to defer entirely to whatever the team prefers:

- `@types/*` as *optional* peer dependencies, so they deduplicate against whatever the consumer already has. Optional matters, otherwise JavaScript-only consumers get unmet-peer warnings.
- Real runtime modules as plain `dependencies`, pinned to whatever already resolves today, with no version bumps.
- `@strapi/*` cross-references as optional peers rather than dependencies, so a second copy of `@strapi/types` cannot appear. Two copies mean two TypeScript module identities, and a `declare module '@strapi/types/dist/...'` augmentation would then target a file no build loads.

I have this applied on a branch and measured against the reproduction above: errors originating in these packages drop from 139 to 2, implicit-any from unreachable `@types/*` drops from 125 to 0, and a JavaScript-only consumer installed with `strictPeerDependencies: true` reports the same two pre-existing unmet peers as before and no new ones. I can open a PR whenever it is welcome.

Some practical notes for whoever picks this up:

- These packages are not published from a generated or templated `package.json`, so the change belongs in each one. `syncpack` only lints `prod` and `dev` dependency types and ignores non-exact specifiers, so loose peer ranges do not trip `yarn version:check`.
- `@types/codemirror5` is an alias (`npm:@types/codemirror@^5.60.15`). Aliases are not reliably expressible in `peerDependencies`, so that one wants to be a plain dependency, matching the existing `codemirror5` alias.
- `@strapi/core` and `@strapi/admin` both reference `@strapi/strapi` in their declarations, which is circular and cannot simply be declared. Those two need a different approach.
- The two errors that remain after the fix are in `@strapi/admin`'s `SubNav.d.ts` (`Cannot find name 'C'`) and follow from `@strapi/design-system`'s own declarations. That is tracked at strapi/design-system#2046, which has the same problem in `@strapi/design-system`, `@strapi/icons` and `@strapi/ui-primitives`, and additionally references `@radix-ui/react-context` without declaring it.
- #27249 is adjacent but solves a different problem: it declares per-workspace `devDependencies` so the monorepo itself builds under a strict linker, and does not change what the published packages declare.
- Several things reported downstream turned out to be already declared at 5.54.0 and need no action: `json-logic-js` and `passport-local` in `@strapi/admin`, `@koa/router` and `json-logic-js` in `@strapi/types`, `cli-progress` in `@strapi/strapi`, `prismjs` in `@strapi/content-manager`, `undici` in `@strapi/core`, and `@radix-ui/react-context` in `@strapi/admin`.

Refiling #27744, which was auto-closed and routed to the feature-request flow. This is a defect in what is already published rather than a roadmap request, so I have moved the proposed fix down here and left the report itself to the symptom and the reproduction.

- [X] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

### Node Version

22.15.1

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

10.9.2

### Strapi Version

5.54.0 (also confirmed present in 5.51.0 — diffed the `content-releases` package source between the two tags and the relevant code is identical)

### Operating System

macOS (Darwin 24.1.0, arm64)

### Database

SQLite

### Javascript or Typescript

Javascript

### Bug Description

A Content Release can show a "Blocked" status in the admin panel while the entries it contains are actually valid, and the scheduled or manual publish still goes through successfully despite the UI showing Blocked. This contradicts the documented behavior that a Blocked release should not publish.

Root cause, confirmed by reading `packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/release.ts` and `.../utils/index.js`, and reproduced live:

1. Each `ReleaseAction`'s `isEntryValid` field is computed once (via `getDraftEntryValidStatus`) when the action is created, and is only recomputed when that exact document is updated again through the normal update lifecycle (confirmed both directions: an action created against an invalid entry is correctly recomputed to valid after the entry itself is edited to fix the problem).
2. There is no equivalent recompute trigger for a release action's cached `isEntryValid` when the underlying problem is resolved through any channel other than a direct edit to that specific document/locale (for example: a bulk import, a migration, or the condition simply no longer applying without that exact document being re-saved). In that situation the release keeps showing "Blocked" indefinitely.
3. Separately, and this is what actually causes the "publish anyway" symptom: `release.ts`'s `publish()` function does not check the release's `status` field or the stored `isEntryValid` value at all before running. It calls `strapi.documents(contentType).publish(params)` directly for each entry, which performs its own fresh, independent validation at that moment. If the entry is genuinely valid by the time publish runs, it succeeds, regardless of what the release's (stale) displayed status says.

The combination of (1)/(2) and (3) means a release can display "Blocked" from a stale cached flag while still publishing successfully when triggered, either manually or via the cron scheduler, which calls the exact same `publish()` service function with no additional check.

To be clear on what this is *not*: when an entry is genuinely invalid at the moment publish runs, `strapi.documents(contentType).publish()` correctly rejects it (confirmed: a required-field violation returns a 400 ValidationError and the release status becomes "failed", with no data published). So this is not a way to publish genuinely broken content — it's the release's own "Blocked" indicator becoming an unreliable, stale preview of what publish will actually do, which defeats the purpose of the safeguard described in the docs.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a collection type with a required field (e.g. `title: string, required: true`), with Draft & Publish enabled.
2. Create an entry, leave the required field empty, so `isEntryValid` correctly computes to `false`.
3. Add this entry to a Release. Confirm the release now shows status "Blocked" (`GET /content-releases/:id` returns `"status": "blocked"`).
4. Now fix the entry through a means that does **not** go through a normal update on that same document/locale performed via the Content Manager — for example, restore the correct value directly at the database layer, or via a bulk import/migration script that bypasses the Document Service's normal update lifecycle, rather than editing it again in the admin UI.
5. Re-check the release: it still reports `"status": "blocked"` even though the entry's data is now genuinely valid.
6. Trigger the release's publish (`POST /content-releases/:id/publish`, which the scheduler also calls internally with no additional guard). The publish succeeds and the entry is published, even though the release's status still showed "Blocked" immediately beforehand.

(Steps 1–3 and the "no guard in publish()" part of step 6 are directly, repeatedly reproduced. Step 4's exact external-fix channel will vary by setup — we've confirmed the recompute gap exists for edits that don't touch the acted-upon document directly, but have not enumerated every real-world path that leads there.)

### Expected Behavior

Either the release's displayed status should be re-validated at the moment publish actually runs (so it cannot go stale relative to what publish will do), or `publish()` should itself refuse to proceed when the release's own last-known status is "blocked" and re-validate before overriding that. Right now neither happens: the cached flag can go stale, and `publish()` ignores it entirely rather than either trusting it or refreshing it.

### Logs

```shell

```

### Code Snippets

`packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/release.ts` — `publish()` only guards against `lockedRelease.releasedAt` (already published) and `lockedRelease.status === 'failed'`; it never checks `status === 'blocked'` before calling `getFormattedActions()` and publishing each entry.

`packages/core/content-releases/server/src/utils/index.js` — `isEntryValid()` is computed and stored at action-creation/update time; the recompute path (`updateActionsOnUpdate` in `middlewares/documents.ts`) only fires for updates to the exact document/locale the action targets.

### Media

_No response_

### Additional information

Internal ticket: Pylon 10428

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

### Node Version
24.14.0

### Package Manager
npm

### Package Manager Version
11.71.0

### Strapi Version
5.52.2

### Operating System
Docker/Podman/LXC (gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13)

### Database
PostgreSQL 16.2

### Javascript or Typescript
Typescript

### Bug Description
On the admin panel's "Reset Password" page (`/auth/reset-password`, reached via the forgot-password email link), only the "password too short" (min 8 characters) validation error is displayed. Validation errors for missing lowercase letter, missing uppercase letter, or missing number are silently swallowed and never shown to the user.

By contrast, the same password strength rules on the logged-in "Profile" page's Change Password form display correctly.

### Root cause
In `packages/core/admin/admin/src/pages/Auth/components/ResetPassword.tsx`, the `lowercase`/`uppercase`/`number` yup `.test()` calls pass an incorrectly nested message descriptor:

```ts
.test(
  'lowercase',
  {
    message: {
      id: 'components.Input.error.contain.lowercase',
      defaultMessage: 'Password must contain at least 1 lowercase letter',
    },
  },
  (value) => (value ? /[a-z]/.test(value) : true)
)
```

yup's `ValidationError.message` becomes this object as-is, so the error gets stored as `{ message: { id, defaultMessage } }` instead of `{ id, defaultMessage }`. `Field.Error` / `formatMessage()` expects the descriptor directly (`{ id, defaultMessage }`), so it cannot resolve the message and nothing is rendered.

The correct pattern is used in `packages/core/admin/admin/src/pages/Settings/pages/Users/utils/validation.ts` (`COMMON_USER_SCHEMA`, used by the Profile page):

```ts
.test(
  'lowercase',
  {
    id: 'components.Input.error.contain.lowercase',
    defaultMessage: 'Password must contain at least one lowercase character',
  },
  (value) => (value ? /[a-z]/.test(value) : true)
)
```

This regression appears to have been introduced by #24538, which fixed the raw-regex-in-error-message issue (#24528) for `validation.ts` and added a workaround in `Register.tsx`'s submit handler to normalize both message shapes, but did not apply the same fix (schema format or handler workaround) to `ResetPassword.tsx`. As a result, `ResetPassword.tsx` still uses the old, incorrectly nested `.test()` message shape, and unlike `Register.tsx`, has no fallback handling to normalize it before rendering.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Trigger a password reset email and open the "Reset Password" link to reach `/auth/reset-password`.
2. Enter a password that is 8+ characters long but missing an uppercase letter, lowercase letter, or number (e.g. `password123` is missing uppercase, or `PASSWORD123` is missing lowercase).
3. Submit the form.
4. Observe that no validation error is shown for the missing character class, even though the request is blocked.

### Expected Behavior
All password validation errors (minimum length, lowercase, uppercase, number, confirm-password mismatch) should be displayed on the Reset Password page, consistent with the Profile page's Change Password form.

### Code Snippets
See "Root cause" section above for the relevant excerpts from `ResetPassword.tsx` and `validation.ts`.

### Additional information
Related: #24528, #24538 (this PR appears to have introduced the regression by fixing `validation.ts` and `Register.tsx` but missing `ResetPassword.tsx`). This is a resubmission of #27693, which was auto-closed because the confirmation checklist checkboxes were not checked in the original submission.

### Confirmation Checklist
- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

### Node Version

22.23.2

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

10.9.8

### Strapi Version

5.54.0

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

Other

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

I ran [Are The Types Wrong](https://arethetypeswrong.github.io/) (`@arethetypeswrong/cli@0.18.5`) against all 37 published packages. I checked two builds: the 5.54.0 versions on npm, and a local pack of `develop` (`yarn setup`, then `attw --pack`). **Both builds give identical results.** 28 packages have at least one problem.

The two main problems:

- **🎭 Masquerading as CJS** ([`FalseCJS`](https://github.com/arethetypeswrong/arethetypeswrong.github.io/blob/main/docs/problems/FalseCJS.md)) in 19 packages
- **❗️ Incorrect default export** ([`FalseExportDefault`](https://github.com/arethetypeswrong/arethetypeswrong.github.io/blob/main/docs/problems/FalseExportDefault.md)) in 21 packages

Both break TypeScript users on `moduleResolution: node16`/`nodenext`. TypeScript 6 deprecates `moduleResolution: node`/`node10` (see #25861), so more projects will hit these problems. They will also block any future move of Strapi itself to ESM.

A few smaller problems are hard failures that affect every consumer, whatever their configuration.

#### 1. 🎭 Masquerading as CJS (`FalseCJS`)

Every affected entry in `exports` shares one `.d.ts` between the `import` and `require` conditions:

```json
".": {
  "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
  "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
  "require": "./dist/index.js"
}
```

The packages have no `"type": "module"`, so TypeScript reads `dist/index.d.ts` as a CommonJS declaration file. An ESM consumer loads the real ESM build (`index.mjs`), but TypeScript types it as CommonJS.

The cause is the build itself: `build:code` runs Rollup and emits `.js` and `.mjs`, then `build:types` runs `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` once. That produces a single `.d.ts`, with no declaration file for each format.

| Package | Affected entrypoints |
| --- | --- |
| `@strapi/core` | `.` |
| `@strapi/strapi` | `.`, `./admin`, `./admin/test` |
| `@strapi/types` | `.` |
| `@strapi/openapi` | `.` |
| `@strapi/upgrade` | `.` |
| `@strapi/admin` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-admin/ee`, `./strapi-admin/test`, `./_internal`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/content-manager` | `./strapi-admin`, `./_internal/shared` |
| `@strapi/content-type-builder` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/content-releases` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/review-workflows` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/email` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/upload` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/i18n` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/plugin-cloud` | `./strapi-admin` |
| `@strapi/plugin-color-picker` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/plugin-documentation` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/plugin-graphql` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/plugin-sentry` | `./strapi-admin`, `./strapi-server` |
| `@strapi/provider-email-nodemailer` | `.` |

#### 2. ❗️ Incorrect default export (`FalseExportDefault`)

The declaration file uses `export default`, but the CommonJS build uses `module.exports = ...`. TypeScript then expects an extra `.default` property, which is `undefined` at runtime.

- All providers: `@strapi/provider-email-amazon-ses`, `provider-email-mailgun`, `provider-email-nodemailer`, `provider-email-sendgrid`, `provider-email-sendmail`, `provider-upload-aws-s3`, `provider-upload-cloudinary`, `provider-upload-local`
- `./strapi-admin` and `./strapi-server`: `@strapi/email`, `content-releases`, `review-workflows`, `upload`, `i18n`, `plugin-color-picker`, `plugin-documentation`, `plugin-graphql`, `plugin-sentry`
- `./strapi-admin` only: `@strapi/plugin-cloud`
- `./strapi-server` only: `@strapi/admin`, `content-manager`, `content-type-builder`

#### 3. 💀 `@strapi/upload/_internal/shared` does not resolve

This subpath fails in **every** resolution mode (`node10`, `node16-cjs`, `node16-esm`, `bundler`), for both types and JavaScript.

The export points to `source: ./shared/index.ts`, but `packages/core/upload/shared/` only contains `constants.ts` and `contracts/`. So `dist/shared/index.{js,mjs,d.ts}` is never built. Nothing in the repository imports `@strapi/upload/_internal/shared`, so the subpath is either dead or missing its entry file.

#### 4. ❌ `create-strapi-app` ships no reachable types (`UntypedResolution`)

`package.json` has `"types": "./dist/src/index.d.ts"`, but that file does not exist. The build emits `dist/index.d.ts`. As a result, every resolution mode resolves JavaScript without types.

#### 5. 🕵️ `@strapi/cloud-cli` named exports (`NamedExports`)

`dist/index.d.ts` declares the named exports `cloudApiFactory` and `VERSION`. Node cannot detect these on the CommonJS `dist/index.js` when importing it from ESM, so `import { cloudApiFactory, VERSION } from '@strapi/cloud-cli'` type-checks but fails at runtime.

#### 6. ❗️ Missing `export =` (`MissingExportEquals`)

In `./strapi-admin` of `@strapi/content-manager` and `@strapi/content-type-builder`, Are The Types Wrong reports that the CommonJS JavaScript (`dist/admin/index.js`) does not match `dist/admin/src/index.d.ts`, which it expects to use `export =`.

#### 7. 💀 `node10` resolution fails for subpath exports (`NoResolution`, `node10` only)

`moduleResolution: node10` ignores `exports`, and there is no `typesVersions` fallback. This only affects the deprecated `node10` mode:

- `./strapi-admin` and `./strapi-server` of every plugin-style package: `admin`, `content-manager`, `content-type-builder`, `content-releases`, `review-workflows`, `email`, `upload`, `i18n`, `plugin-cloud` (`./strapi-admin` only), `plugin-color-picker`, `plugin-documentation`, `plugin-graphql`, `plugin-sentry`
- `@strapi/admin`: `./strapi-admin/ee`, `./strapi-admin/test`, `./_internal`
- `@strapi/content-manager`: `./_internal/shared`
- `@strapi/strapi`: `./admin`, `./admin/test`
- `@strapi/provider-email-nodemailer`: `./utils`

#### Clean or not applicable

- No problems: `@strapi/data-transfer`, `@strapi/database`, `@strapi/permissions`, `@strapi/utils`, `@strapi/generators`, `@strapi/logger`, `@strapi/typescript-utils`
- No types shipped: `create-strapi`, `@strapi/plugin-users-permissions`

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check any package:
   ```sh
   npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --from-npm @strapi/provider-email-nodemailer
   ```
   ```
   "@strapi/provider-email-nodemailer"
   node10: ❗️ Incorrect default export
   node16 (from CJS): ❗️ Incorrect default export
   node16 (from ESM): 🎭 Masquerading as CJS
   bundler: 🟢
   ```

2. For concrete failures, create an ESM TypeScript project:
   ```sh
   npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
   npm i @strapi/provider-email-nodemailer@5.54.0 @strapi/provider-email-sendmail@5.54.0 typescript@5.9.3 @types/node
   ```

   `tsconfig.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "compilerOptions": {
       "module": "nodenext",
       "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
       "target": "es2022",
       "strict": true,
       "skipLibCheck": true,
       "noEmit": true
     }
   }
   ```

   `nodemailer.ts` (Masquerading as CJS: the package has an `import` condition that points to `.mjs`):
   ```ts
   import provider from '@strapi/provider-email-nodemailer';

   console.log(typeof provider.init);
   ```

   `sendmail.ts` (Incorrect default export: the package is CommonJS only):
   ```ts
   import provider from '@strapi/provider-email-sendmail';

   console.log(typeof provider.init);
   ```

3. Run `npx tsc -p .`. Both files fail:
   ```
   nodemailer.ts(3,29): error TS2339: Property 'init' does not exist on type 'typeof import(".../node_modules/@strapi/provider-email-nodemailer/dist/index")'.
   sendmail.ts(3,29): error TS2339: Property 'init' does not exist on type 'typeof import(".../node_modules/@strapi/provider-email-sendmail/dist/index")'.
   ```

4. Run the same code with Node as `.mjs`. Both files print `function`, so the code is correct at runtime.

5. The spelling TypeScript accepts, `provider.default.init`, is `undefined` at runtime (`typeof provider.default` is `'undefined'`).

### Expected Behavior

- `npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --pack <package>` reports no problems for any published package, or at most the `node10` subpath limitation.
- Declaration files match the JavaScript file each condition loads. ESM consumers get ESM declarations (`.d.mts`), and CommonJS consumers get CommonJS declarations (`.d.ts`/`.d.cts`) whose default export uses `export =` to match `module.exports`.
- Every subpath listed in `exports` exists in the published tarball.

For example, the exports map could nest `types` inside each condition:

```json
".": {
  "import": {
    "types": "./dist/index.d.mts",
    "default": "./dist/index.mjs"
  },
  "require": {
    "types": "./dist/index.d.cts",
    "default": "./dist/index.cjs"
  }
}
```

### Logs

_No response_

### Code Snippets

_No response_

### Media

_No response_

### Additional information

#### Suggested direction

Problems 1, 2, 5 and 6 all come from generating declarations separately from the format-specific JavaScript builds. Copying `.d.ts` to `.d.mts` is not enough, because relative imports inside a `.d.mts` need explicit extensions under `nodenext`.

A build tool that emits declarations for each output format would fix these together. For example, [tsdown](https://tsdown.dev/) with `format: ['esm', 'cjs']` and `dts: true` emits `.d.mts` and `.d.cts`, and can generate the `exports` map. Points to validate when migrating:

- **`@strapi/types` module augmentation.** Bundled declarations may break `declare module '@strapi/types/...'` augmentation and the `./*` wildcard export, so that package may need unbundled declarations.
- **`strapi-admin` entries.** These use React, CSS and assets, plus the `source` condition that the shared Rollup config handles today.
- **Declaration build time.** Without `isolatedDeclarations`, declarations are generated by the TypeScript compiler.

Problems 3 and 4 are independent fixes: add or remove the `./_internal/shared` entry, and correct the `types` path.

Running `attw --pack` in CI, even as a non-blocking check at first, would stop regressions and track progress.

#### Scope

The `develop` pack was built from commit `008e09571f`. Its `package.json` versions still read 5.53.0, but the results match 5.54.0 on npm exactly.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

### Javascript or Typescript

### Bug Description

## TLDR: 
`/packages/utils/typescript/tsconfigs/server.json` should have `strict: true` to align with default project settings

## Explanations
I'm working on the migration to v5 of a v4 project that had been initialized with the following root `tsconfig.json` : 
```jsonc
{
  "extends": "@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/server",
  "compilerOptions": {
  // ...
```
I had weird TS behavior in my project (wrong type inference) and when inspecting the content of the `@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/server` file, I saw that it had strict mode set to false :
https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/aa62644810e48c3b65e4b15e1055b97cd1c158fa/packages/utils/typescript/tsconfigs/server.json#L10

When initializing a fresh new v5 project with `npx create-strapi`, the generated tsconfig doesn't use this extend, and contains this :
```jsonc
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "CommonJS",
    "moduleResolution": "Node",
    "lib": ["ES2020"],
    "target": "ES2019",
    "strict": true, // 👈 this is the only difference with `typescript-utils/tsconfigs/server`
    "skipLibCheck": true,
```

### Node Version

22.23.2

### Package Manager

pnpm

### Package Manager Version

10.x (also reproduced with yarn 4.12.0)

### Strapi Version

5.52.0 (config unchanged on `develop` @ 5.53.0)

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Bug Description

`packages/utils/typescript/tsconfigs/server.json` ships a **relative** `tsBuildInfoFile`:

```json
"tsBuildInfoFile": "./.tsbuildinfo",
"incremental": true
```

A relative `tsBuildInfoFile` resolves against the tsconfig that **declares** it, not the one being compiled. That declaring file ships inside the published package, so every project extending `@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/server` writes its build info to the same path **inside `node_modules`**:

```
node_modules/@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/.tsbuildinfo
```

Consequences:

1. **Incremental never pays off.** Multiple projects share one file, last-writer-wins. Each build reads a buildinfo describing a *different* program, TypeScript discards it and does a full build. Pure overhead, never a speedup.
2. **It writes into a dependency directory.** Under pnpm, `.pnpm/**` is meant to be immutable content-addressed storage — a stray file there is wiped by reinstall/store prune and can make the package look modified. Under npm/yarn it is the same class of problem, just less strictly enforced.
3. **`.gitignore` cannot reach it** — it is inside `node_modules`.

Observed in a monorepo with four Strapi plugin server projects + one CMS app, all extending this base. All four plugins wrote to:

```
node_modules/.pnpm/@strapi+typescript-utils@5.52.0/node_modules/@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/.tsbuildinfo
```

One 180.8 KB file containing 756 `fileNames` — exactly one project's program, whichever compiled last.

This is not limited to plugin builds. Strapi's own compile path hits it too: `resolveConfigOptions` → `ts.getParsedCommandLineOfConfigFile` resolves the option to the package path, and `ts.createProgram(...).emit()` in `packages/utils/typescript/src/compilers/basic.ts` writes the file there. So any TypeScript Strapi app running `strapi build` / `strapi develop` writes into `node_modules` as well.

The option was added in #20341 (commit 7f81f32, 2024-05-20, DX-1400) to silence `TS5074: Option '--incremental' can only be specified using tsconfig, emitting to single file or when option '--tsBuildInfoFile' is specified.` — see "Additional information" for whether that is still needed.

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal repro, no Strapi needed (verified on TypeScript 5.9.3, the version `@strapi/typescript-utils` pins):

```
base/tsconfig.json  { "compilerOptions": { "incremental": true, "tsBuildInfoFile": "./.tsbuildinfo" } }
proj/tsconfig.json  { "extends": "../base/tsconfig.json", "include": ["./src"],
                      "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "./dist", "rootDir": "./src" } }
proj/src/a.ts       export const a = 1;

$ tsc -p proj/tsconfig.json
```

Result: `base/.tsbuildinfo` — i.e. the *declaring* config's directory.

Three variants, same input:

| `base` declares | build info lands at |
| --- | --- |
| `"tsBuildInfoFile": "./.tsbuildinfo"` | `base/.tsbuildinfo` ❌ |
| *(option omitted)* | `proj/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` ✅ |
| `"tsBuildInfoFile": "${configDir}/.tsbuildinfo"` | `proj/.tsbuildinfo` ✅ |

TypeScript's own default is already per-project and correct. The explicit `"./"` is strictly worse than omitting it. (The docs' "Default: `.tsbuildinfo`" is a simplification — the real default is derived from the consuming project's `outDir` / config name.)

Against the real config, using Strapi's own resolution path:

```js
const ts = require('typescript');
// tsconfig.json extends "@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/server"
const { errors, ...c } = ts.getParsedCommandLineOfConfigFile('tsconfig.json', undefined, ts.sys);
console.log(c.options.tsBuildInfoFile);
// .../node_modules/@strapi/typescript-utils/tsconfigs/.tsbuildinfo
ts.createProgram({ rootNames: c.fileNames, options: c.options }).emit();
// writes that file inside the package
```

### Expected Behavior

Each consuming project writes its own build info inside its own directory (next to its `outDir`), so incremental compilation actually works per project and nothing is ever written into `node_modules`.

### Additional information

Two possible fixes — maintainers' pick:

**a) Use `${configDir}` (TS ≥ 5.5), which expands to the consuming config's directory:**

```json
"tsBuildInfoFile": "${configDir}/.tsbuildinfo"
```

Keeps an explicit value, still silences TS5074, and is per-project. `@strapi/typescript-utils` depends on `typescript@5.9.3`, so the feature is available; consumers on their own TypeScript would need ≥ 5.5.

**b) Remove `tsBuildInfoFile` entirely** and rely on TypeScript's default, which is already per-project.

One caveat on (b): the original TS5074 from #20341 *still reproduces* on TypeScript 5.9.3, but only when the compiler options do not come from a config file. Verified:

```js
ts.createProgram({ rootNames: ['a.ts'], options: { incremental: true, outDir: 'out' } });
// diagnostic 5074

ts.createProgram({ rootNames: ['a.ts'], options: { incremental: true, outDir: 'out', configFilePath: '/abs/tsconfig.json' } });
// no diagnostics
```

So `configFilePath` also silences it. For consumers running `tsc -p tsconfig.json` (or Strapi's own `resolveConfigOptions`, which sets `configFilePath`), removal is safe; for a tool that merges the options in programmatically without `configFilePath`, removal would bring the error back. That makes **(a) the lower-risk fix** — it fixes the path and keeps the diagnostic silenced in both shapes.

Happy to open a PR for whichever option you prefer.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing issues for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct.
items.title: @strapi/typescript-utils ships a relative tsBuildInfoFile, so every consuming project writes build info into node_modules

### Node Version

22.23.2

### Package Manager

yarn

### Package Manager Version

4.12.0

### Strapi Version

5.53.0

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

SQLite

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

https://github.com/strapi/strapi

### Bug Description

Every Strapi CLI command that loads the application (`routes:list`, `content-types:list`, `admin:*`, `configuration:dump`, `openapi:generate`, `export`, `import`, `transfer`, `console`, `report`, …) calls `compileStrapi()` first, which runs an incremental TypeScript compilation of the whole project into `dist`.

There is no way to opt out of this step. That becomes a problem in several situations:

- **Running commands in parallel is unsafe.** Each process compiles the same project into the same `outDir` (and the same `tsbuildinfo`) at the same time, so concurrent invocations race on writing identical files.
- **Deployed apps get rebuilt.** On a deployed server (for example after SSH-ing in to run a one-off command such as `strapi admin:reset-user-password` or `strapi configuration:dump`), the command first recompiles the project in place. That overwrites the deployed build output and requires the TypeScript toolchain and sources to be present, which is not desirable in production.
- **Redundant work.** In CI or scripts that already ran `strapi build`, every subsequent command recompiles the project again, even though the build output is up to date.

`strapi start` already reuses the existing build output without compiling, but the other app-loading commands have no equivalent.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create or use a TypeScript Strapi project.
2. Run `strapi build`.
3. Run several app-loading commands in parallel, for example:
   ```bash
   strapi routes:list &
   strapi content-types:list &
   strapi configuration:dump -f config.json &
   wait
   ```
4. Each process runs its own TypeScript compilation into the same `dist` directory concurrently.

### Expected Behavior

It should be possible to build once and then run CLI commands against the existing build output, for example with a flag and/or environment variable:

```bash
strapi build
strapi routes:list --skip-compile &
strapi content-types:list --skip-compile &
STRAPI_SKIP_COMPILE=true strapi configuration:dump -f config.json &
wait
```

When skipping, the command should reuse the resolved `outDir` and fail with a clear message if the build output does not exist (same behaviour as `strapi start`).

### Additional information

Proposed implementation (draft: unrevised6419/strapi#16):

- `compileStrapi()` accepts a `skipCompile` option, defaulting to `process.env.STRAPI_SKIP_COMPILE === 'true'`. When set, it skips `tsUtils.compile` and throws if the `outDir` is missing.
- The CLI registers a global `--skip-compile` option that sets `STRAPI_SKIP_COMPILE=true`, so every command that goes through `compileStrapi()` picks it up without per-command changes. `build` and `develop` do not use `compileStrapi()` and are unaffected.

#### Benchmarks

Wall-clock time of `npx strapi content-types:list` with and without `--skip-compile`, using the draft implementation (`2a68712f11`) with packages built. Node v22.23.2, macOS 26.6.2, Apple M1 (8 cores), 16 GB. Output discarded, 1 warmup run, then 2 rounds of 15 runs per variant. The command does not connect to the database, so the database is not part of the timings.

**`examples/complex`** (TypeScript)

| Round | Variant | mean | median | min | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--skip-compile` | 1.391s | 1.320s | 1.245s | 1.988s |
| 1 | compile (warm) | 2.577s | 2.539s | 2.438s | 3.204s |
| 2 | `--skip-compile` | 1.271s | 1.263s | 1.251s | 1.313s |
| 2 | compile (warm) | 2.764s | 2.597s | 2.483s | 4.311s |
| – | compile (cold, n=10) | 2.589s | 2.583s | 2.516s | 2.689s |

"Warm" means `dist/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` is present and sources are unchanged; "cold" deletes it before each run. Cold and warm are about the same, so the incremental build info saves almost nothing here.

**`examples/kitchensink-ts`** (TypeScript): medians of 1.240s / 1.302s with `--skip-compile` vs 2.426s / 2.470s compiling.

**`examples/getstarted`** (JavaScript): no difference (about 1.5s either way), as expected since JavaScript projects are never compiled.

Summary: compiling adds about 1.2–1.3s to every command in a TypeScript project, roughly doubling the time of a short command such as `content-types:list` (these timings include `npx` startup). Parallel runs were not benchmarked.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

items.body:
### Node Version

22.x

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

11.16.0

### Strapi Version

5.46.0 (reported). Verified still present on 5.53.0 and on `develop`.

### Operating System

Strapi Cloud

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL



### Bug Description

When a GraphQL client aborts a request — an `AbortController`, a client-side timeout, or simply a closed connection — Strapi keeps executing the operation to completion. Every resolver runs, every relation-population query is issued, and a connection from the shared pool stays checked out for the whole duration, long after there is anybody left to receive the response.

There is no cancellation path at any layer of the request chain:

- **`@strapi/plugin-graphql` is pinned to `graphql: ^16.8.1`** (`packages/plugins/graphql/package.json`). graphql-js 16 has no cancellation API at all — `execute()` accepts no `abortSignal`. Verified against the installed `graphql@16.14.0`: zero occurrences of `abortSignal` in `execution/execute.js`.
- The Apollo integration (`new ApolloServer(...)` + `@as-integrations/koa@1.1.1`, `packages/plugins/graphql/server/src/bootstrap.ts`) never registers a `close`/`aborted` listener on `ctx.req`, and has no per-request cancellation of its own.
- `createHTTPServer` (`packages/core/core/src/services/server/http-server.ts`) tracks sockets only so `destroy()` can close them at shutdown. Node emits the disconnect on `ctx.req`, but nothing downstream acts on it.
- `@strapi/database` never calls knex's `.timeout()` (zero occurrences in `packages/core/database/src`), so there is no per-query ceiling to fall back on either — even though the pinned `knex@3.0.1` does implement `cancelQuery()` for Postgres (`pg_cancel_backend`).

The consequence is that abandoned work is indistinguishable from live work. A burst of GraphQL requests that clients have already given up on still occupies the connection pool (`pool.max` defaults to 10). Requests that arrive afterwards queue behind work nobody is waiting for, exceed `acquireConnectionTimeout` (default 60s) and fail with:

```
Knex: Timeout acquiring a connection. The pool is probably full.
```

REST requests fail alongside them, because the pool is shared. The instance does not recover on its own while the client keeps retrying — each retry adds another uncancellable operation — and only clears when the process is restarted.

This was observed in production on a Cloud instance: a front-end regeneration fired site-wide GraphQL queries across several locales at once; the client abandoned requests after its own 10s/30s timeouts and retried them; the server carried on executing every abandoned operation to completion. Over the two-hour window 23% of all HTTP responses were 500s, median response time sat between 2 and 9 minutes, and the longest single response was just under 20 minutes. It ended when the customer manually redeployed, not on its own.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a fresh Strapi 5 project on PostgreSQL with `@strapi/plugin-graphql` installed.
2. Make a GraphQL operation that takes measurably long — either a content type with enough nested relations that population takes several seconds, or a custom resolver that awaits `strapi.db.connection.raw('select pg_sleep(30)')`.
3. In `config/database.ts`, set `pool: { min: 0, max: 2 }` so exhaustion is visible immediately rather than at scale.
4. Fire a handful of concurrent GraphQL requests and abort each one after a second, i.e. before the server can answer:

   ```bash
   for i in 1 2 3; do
     curl --max-time 1 -s -X POST http://localhost:1337/graphql \
       -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
       -d '{"query":"{ slowQuery { documentId } }"}' &
   done
   wait
   ```

5. Immediately after the clients have gone, inspect the database:

   ```sql
   select pid, state, now() - query_start as running_for, left(query, 60)
   from pg_stat_activity where state <> 'idle';
   ```

6. Observe that the queries are still running and the connections are still checked out, with no client attached to any of them. Send one ordinary request while they are still in flight and it fails with `Knex: Timeout acquiring a connection. The pool is probably full.`

### Expected Behavior

When the client disconnects or aborts, Strapi should stop doing work for that request:

- GraphQL execution should stop at the next field boundary instead of resolving the remainder of the tree,
- the in-flight database query should be cancelled rather than run to completion (`knex`'s `.timeout(ms, { cancel: true })` issues `pg_cancel_backend` on Postgres),
- the pooled connection should be returned promptly, so abandoned work cannot starve live traffic.

graphql-js v17 — `latest` on npm since 2026-06-15 — added exactly the missing primitive: `graphql()`, `execute()`, `subscribe()` and `experimentalExecuteIncrementally()` all accept an `abortSignal`; resolvers can reach a scoped signal through `info.getAbortSignal()` to propagate cancellation to anything downstream; and an aborted execution rejects with `AbortedGraphQLExecutionError` carrying the partial result. Upgrading `@strapi/plugin-graphql` onto v17 and wiring Koa's request-abort into that signal is what this issue is asking for.

### Logs

```shell
error: Knex: Timeout acquiring a connection. The pool is probably full. Are you missing a .transacting(trx) call?
    at Client_PG.acquireConnection
    at async Runner.ensureConnection
    at async Runner.run
    ... @strapi/database entity-manager findOne / load (relation population inside GraphQL resolvers)
```

### Code Snippets

Relevant source, on `develop` (5.53.0 line):

```
packages/plugins/graphql/package.json               "graphql": "^16.8.1", "@apollo/server": "4.13.0", "@as-integrations/koa": "1.1.1"
packages/plugins/graphql/server/src/bootstrap.ts    ApolloServer mounted via koaMiddleware; no signal plumbed through
packages/core/core/src/services/server/http-server.ts   sockets tracked for shutdown destroy() only
packages/core/database/src/                         no call to knex .timeout() anywhere
packages/core/database/src/connection.ts            createConnection() builds knex from user config; no query-timeout default
```

### Additional information

**This is not a one-line dependency bump — the Apollo layer blocks it today:**

- `@apollo/server` latest (5.5.1) still declares `peerDependencies: { "graphql": "^16.11.0" }`. It does not support graphql v17 yet.
- `@as-integrations/koa@3.0.0` (the version that pairs with Apollo Server 5) requires `@apollo/server ^5.0.0` and `koa ^3.0.0`, while `@strapi/core` is on `koa@2.16.4`.

So the v17 upgrade needs a path through Apollo Server and Koa, or a different execution host, rather than a version bump on `graphql` alone.

**Two mitigations are available without v17** and are worth considering independently, since they address the resource-exhaustion half of this directly:

1. Pass a query timeout to knex in `@strapi/database` — `.timeout(ms, { cancel: true })` — so that no single query can outlive its usefulness regardless of what the client did. Configurable, off by default if necessary.
2. Listen for `close`/`aborted` on `ctx.req` in the GraphQL (and REST) request path and stop issuing further database queries for a request whose client has gone, even if the operation already in flight cannot be interrupted.

Internal ticket: Pylon 10303

### Confirmation Checklist

- [X] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [X] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

items.body:
### Node Version

24.0.0

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

10.0.0

### Strapi Version

5.33.0

### Operating System

MacOS

### Database

MySQL

### Javascript or Typescript

Typescript

### Reproduction URL

_No response_

### Bug Description

## Summary

Settings → Internationalization currently has 12 locale codes each
registered twice as separate rows (`en-eg`, `en-bh`, `en-qa`, `en-jo`,
`en-lb`, `en-om`, `ar-eg`, `ar-bh`, `ar-qa`, `ar-jo`, `ar-lb`, `ar-om`), each
pair sharing the identical display name (e.g. two "English-Egypt" rows).
All 12 duplicates were created at the exact same timestamp (2025-06-17
09:58:26), well after the originals (2023-08-02) — consistent with a single
script or migration re-inserting them, not manual duplication.

## The issue

Deleting one row of a duplicate pair does **not** just remove the redundant
configuration entry — it deletes all content saved under that locale code,
including content that predates and is unrelated to the duplicate. This was
confirmed directly: creating a Page under `en-jo`, then deleting one of the
two `en-jo` locale rows, deleted that Page.

This is more destructive than a first look suggests. A database-level check
(`information_schema.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` against `i18n_locales`) shows nothing
has a foreign key on this table's `id`, which would normally suggest a
duplicate row is inert, cosmetic-only data. It isn't: the Internationalization
plugin's delete-locale action appears to clean up content by matching the
locale **code string**, not the specific row's ID — so removing either row
of a pair removes every entry saved under that code, regardless of the
duplicate row that's left behind.

## Impact

- Any admin who tries to "clean up" the locale list by removing what looks
  like a redundant entry will silently delete every Page/Story/etc. saved
  under that locale code, with no confirmation that distinguishes "delete
  this duplicate config row" from "delete all content in this locale."
- No built-in undo. Recovery depends entirely on whether a database backup
  exists from before the deletion.

## Recommendation

- Do not delete any of the remaining 11 duplicate rows without first
  exporting/backing up all content saved under that locale code and
  confirming the backup is restorable.
- Before any cleanup, verify against a restorable environment (not
  production directly) that deleting the intended row does not affect
  content, the same way this issue was originally found.
- Worth filing with Strapi/the `i18n` plugin maintainers if this cascade
  behavior on duplicate codes isn't already a known issue — a delete-locale
  action arguably shouldn't remove content for a code that still has another
  active locale definition pointing at it.

## Testing

- Reproduced directly: created a Page under `en-jo`, deleted one of the two
  `en-jo` locale definitions, confirmed the Page was deleted.
- Confirmed no FK constraint exists on `i18n_locales.id` (ruled out as the
  deletion mechanism; the plugin's own code, not the database, enforces
  this).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Go to **Settings → Internationalization**. Confirm `en-jo` (or any of the
   12 duplicated codes) appears as two separate rows with identical display
   names.
2. Go to **Content Manager → Page**, create a new Page, switch its locale to
   **English-Jordan**, and save/publish it.
3. Return to **Settings → Internationalization**, and delete **either one**
   of the two `en-jo` rows.
4. Go back to the Page created in step 2 and check its `en-jo` locale.

### Expected Behavior

Deleting one of two duplicate locale *configuration* rows should only
remove that redundant entry from the locale list — it should have no effect
on content, since a second row for the same code (`en-jo`) still exists and
the underlying code itself hasn't been removed from the system.

### Logs

```shell

```

### Code Snippets

_No response_

### Media

_No response_

### Additional information

The Page created in step 2 is deleted along with the locale row. Content
saved under a locale code is removed whenever *any* row for that code is
deleted — not scoped to the specific duplicate row being removed, and not
prevented by the fact that another row for the same code still exists.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

This looks intentional in this [commit](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/commit/2f3595fe612ff93ffe08de6b00f07d77f8ac05bd) where `redirectWithPayload` is now called with an empty `{}` payload. ### Node Version

v22.23.1 (reproduction); v20.20.2 (the affected production apps)

### Package Manager

npm

### Package Manager Version

10.9.8 (reproduction); yarn 4.9.4 in the affected production apps

### Strapi Version

5.53.0 (latest); first observed on 5.42.0 and the code is unchanged between them

### Operating System

Linux (Debian 12, kernel 6.1)

### Database

PostgreSQL 16 through `pg@8.23.0` (reproduction); PostgreSQL 17 behind PgBouncer 1.25.1 (transaction pooling) through `pg@8.20.0` (production) — the warning is client-side `pg.Client` state, so the pooler makes no difference

### Javascript or Typescript

Javascript

### Reproduction URL

https://github.com/onyxdevs/strapi-transaction-populate-queue

### Bug Description

Every Document Service read that populates three or more relations issues its populate queries **concurrently on the transaction's single connection**, which node-postgres deprecated in 8.19.0 and removes in 9.0:

```
(node:24) DeprecationWarning: Calling client.query() when the client is already executing a query is deprecated and will be removed in pg@9.0. Use async/await or an external async flow control mechanism instead.
```

The chain in `develop` (identical in 5.42.0 and 5.53.0):

1. `packages/core/core/src/services/document-service/repository.ts` — `findMany: wrapInTransaction(findMany)` (reads are transactional), so `db.transaction()` pins one knex connection and stores it in `transactionCtx`.
2. `packages/core/database/src/query/helpers/populate/apply.ts` — `await Promise.all(Object.keys(populate).map(populateAttribute))` fans every relation out at once (the `morphToMany` branch does the same per target type).
3. `packages/core/database/src/query/query-builder.ts` — `execute()` reads `transactionCtx.get()` and calls `qb.transacting(transaction)`, so every one of those populate queries is sent to the same `pg.Client` while it is still executing the previous one.

`pg` warns only when a query is already *queued* behind the active one (`Client.query`, `if (this._queryQueue.length > 0)`), so a single-relation or two-relation populate stays quiet and the third relation trips it. Outside a transaction (`strapi.db.query(...)`) the same populate spreads across the pool and nothing is queued.

Today `pg@8` still queues the extra queries, so the warning is the only visible effect. node-postgres has already merged the removal (brianc/node-postgres#3603, "we're removing it in 9.x"), after which the same read throws — for every Strapi + Postgres app, on its most common read path.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone https://github.com/onyxdevs/strapi-transaction-populate-queue and start a Postgres: `docker run -d --rm --name pgrepro -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=repro -e POSTGRES_DB=repro -p 127.0.0.1:55432:5432 postgres:16-alpine`
2. `npm install`
3. `DATABASE_PORT=55432 npm run repro` — boots Strapi without the HTTP server, seeds one `post` with an `author`, a `category` and a `tag`, runs `strapi.documents('api::post.post').findMany({ populate: ['author', 'category', 'tags'], limit: 1 })` under `--trace-deprecation`.
4. Alternatively `NODE_OPTIONS=--trace-deprecation npm run develop` and `GET /api/posts?populate=*`.

### Expected Behavior

A transactional read populates its relations without sending a second query to a client that is still executing one — either sequentially on the transaction connection (which is what the driver was doing internally anyway) or outside the transaction — so nothing changes when `pg@9` lands.

### Logs

```
[warning] DeprecationWarning: Calling client.query() when the client is already executing a query is deprecated and will be removed in pg@9.0. Use async/await or an external async flow control mechanism instead.
    at Client.query (node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:762:7)
    at node_modules/knex/lib/dialects/postgres/index.js:226:18
    at Client_PG._query (node_modules/knex/lib/dialects/postgres/index.js:225:12)
    at executeQuery (node_modules/knex/lib/execution/internal/query-executioner.js:37:17)
    at Client_PG.query (node_modules/knex/lib/client.js:154:12)
    at node_modules/knex/lib/execution/transaction.js:371:24
    at trxClient.query (node_modules/knex/lib/execution/transaction.js:366:12)
    at Runner.query (node_modules/knex/lib/execution/runner.js:141:36)
findMany returned 1 post(s) with relations: author, category, tags
node-postgres deprecation warnings emitted: 1
```

### Code Snippets

A driver-level demonstration that isolates the mechanism (knex 3.0.1, the version Strapi pins), run with `node --trace-deprecation`:

```js
// three concurrent queries on the POOL: no warning
await Promise.all([knex.raw('select 1'), knex.raw('select 2'), knex.raw('select 3')]);
// three concurrent queries inside ONE transaction: the warning, from the third query
await knex.transaction((trx) => Promise.all([trx.raw('select 1'), trx.raw('select 2'), trx.raw('select 3')]));
// the same three, awaited one after another inside the transaction: no warning
```

### Additional information

- Measured on a production app with the populate loop made sequential under an active transaction: 20 transactional `findMany` calls populating 5 relations took 262–331 ms both before and after, i.e. no throughput change, because `pg` was already serialising those queries on the one connection.
- A pull request with the fix (sequential populate only when `transactionCtx.get()` is set, parallel fan-out unchanged otherwise) and a unit test that fails on `develop` follows.

### Confirmation Checklist

- [x] I have checked the existing [issues](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/issues) for duplicates.
- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

MacOS
